headline: Buying Quality Stocks at the 200-Week Moving Average
lede: A tweet from @r6ride_87 notes that Microsoft (MSFT) is currently trading at its 200-week moving average, and argues that buying high-quality stocks at this level has historically beaten the S&P 500. The strategy, often attributed to Charlie Munger, relies on discipline few investors possess.
body:
The 200-week moving average is a long-term trend line that smooths out price fluctuations over nearly four years. When a stock like Microsoft (MSFT) touches this level, it often signals that the market has priced in significant pessimism. The claim that buying high-quality stocks at the 200-week moving average outperforms the S&P 500 over time is supported by backtests, but it requires investors to act against their emotions—buying when fear is highest.

This approach is frequently linked to Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett's longtime partner, who emphasized buying wonderful businesses at fair prices. The 200-week moving average serves as a rough proxy for "fair price" when applied to quality companies. However, the strategy is not a mechanical formula: it depends on correctly identifying which stocks are "high-quality," a subjective judgment that can lead to value traps.

The tweet's specific mention of Microsoft is timely. The stock has underperformed in 2025 amid concerns about AI spending and slowing cloud growth. Yet Microsoft remains a dominant enterprise software and cloud player, with a strong balance sheet and wide moat. Whether the 200-week moving average marks a bottom or just a pause depends on fundamentals, not just technicals.

Investors should note that the 200-week moving average strategy works best with a diversified basket of quality stocks, not a single name. Even then, drawdowns can be severe and prolonged. The real edge, as the tweet implies, is behavioral: the discipline to buy when others are selling.

concepts.definition: A technical indicator that calculates the average closing price of a stock over the past 200 weeks (roughly four years). It is used to identify long-term trends and potential support or resistance levels.

Shares of companies with strong competitive advantages, consistent earnings, solid balance sheets, and reliable management. Examples include blue-chip firms like Microsoft, Apple, and Johnson & Johnson.
A stock that appears cheap based on valuation metrics but is actually a poor investment because the underlying business is deteriorating. Investors who buy such stocks may see further declines.
